_README: Research highlights — the scientific feed on the Research page.
This is the section modelled on how experimental groups present their work:
newest first, each entry a figure, a title, and a short technical summary.
It is written for colleagues, not for the general reader - the rest of the
Research page does the plain-language job.
Copy a block below, put it at the TOP of the list, and fill it in.
date     a short label, e.g. 'October 2026'. Free text.
body     the summary. Two or three sentences is right.
image    a file in images/web/  (optional - leave as "" for no figure)
link     URL to the paper, preprint or project page (optional)
linkText what the link should say (optional, defaults to 'Read the paper')
tag      small label above the title, e.g. 'Publication', 'Instrument',
Entries are shown in the order they appear here. Newest at the top.
image    a file in images/web/. Files starting with 'fig-' are line drawings and are shown on a white plate, uncropped.

notes.title: Mössbauer spectroscopy at ESRF ID14
notes.body: A week on ID14 at the European Synchrotron, using nuclear resonant scattering to determine the oxidation state and coordination environment of iron in silicate glasses and melts. Iron redox is one of the strongest single controls on melt viscosity and on crystallisation behaviour, and it remains difficult to measure in situ at magmatic temperatures. Proposal ES-1817.

notes.title: Where carbonatite magmas come from
notes.body: An experimental study of the origin of carbonatites, at CRPG in Nancy. Starting from the composition of the parental magma of Oldoinyo Lengai, the only active carbonatite volcano, the magma was crystallised step by step in a piston cylinder at lower-crustal pressure, removing the crystals each time and carrying the residual liquid on, until droplets of carbonate melt separated from it. Letting the same magma crystallise in one go never gets there. Fractional crystallisation of a common magma is enough; no carbon-rich mantle is needed. With Lydéric France, Pierre Condamine, Célia Dalou and Marie-Camille Caumon.

notes.title: Viscosity of trachytic melt from the Agnano–Monte Spina eruption, Campi Flegrei
notes.body: Calorimetry, viscometry and in situ Raman and Brillouin spectroscopy combined on the Agnano–Monte Spina trachyte. The melt begins to reorganise at the nanoscale within minutes above its glass transition, so standard viscometry can overestimate its viscosity by up to a log unit; a model built around that shows a hundred-thousand-fold stiffening as the melt loses its water — ten times earlier estimates — with consequences for degassing, fragmentation and eruptive style. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth.

notes.title: Superheating controls clinopyroxene nucleation delay in mafic magmas
notes.body: In situ synchrotron observation of crystallisation in mafic melts shows that superheating delays clinopyroxene nucleation, so ascending magma stays less crystalline than equilibrium would predict. Because crystal content governs viscosity, and viscosity governs whether a conduit erupts gently or explosively, the delay has direct consequences for ascent dynamics. Nature Communications.

notes.title: AVEXT-3D, the data: pore networks from 27 tomograms (EXCITE2)
notes.body: The follow-up: twenty days of remote data-processing access at CEITEC to segment the scanned volumes and extract porosity, bubble number density, connectivity, tortuosity and throat-to-pore ratios for every sample. Those numbers feed the conduit model of La Spina et al. (2022), which is where microtexture turns into a statement about eruptive style — from the effusive to the paroxysmal, across basalt, basanite, trachyte and rhyolite.

notes.title: Phase-contrast microtomography at ESRF BM18
notes.body: Three-dimensional imaging of volcanic products at BM18, resolving vesicle networks and crystal textures without sectioning the sample. Porosity and its connectivity determine whether gas escapes from a magma or pressurises it, and that is only visible in three dimensions. Proposal ES-1647.

notes.title: AVEXT-3D — volcanic rock textures by 3D X-ray microtomography (EXCITE2)
notes.body: Transnational-access project at CEITEC, Brno, funded through the EXCITE2 network: twenty-seven samples — pumice and scoria from Stromboli, Vulcano and Lipari, and run products from controlled decompression experiments in a cold-seal vessel — scanned at a voxel size of about 1.5 µm on the phoenix v|tome|x L240, fine enough to resolve the 2–3 µm glass films between neighbouring bubbles. Whether gas escapes a rising magma or builds until it fragments is decided in that pore network.

notes.title: HYDROETNA — glass and melt properties of hydrous Etna trachybasalt
notes.body: Awarded through ILGE-TNA/NOA 2025, hosted at the National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology in Rome. Dissolved water lowers the viscosity of a silicate melt by orders of magnitude, so quantifying it in Etna trachybasalt is a prerequisite for any realistic model of how that system erupts.

notes.title: Calibrating the DSC shift-factor approach between laboratories
notes.body: Differential scanning calorimetry offers a fast route to melt viscosity near the glass transition, but the shift-factor approach it depends on had not been shown to give consistent results across laboratories. Using lead metasilicate glass as a common reference, this work established that calibration, together with a parallel study on Na₂O-enriched and aluminium-bearing haplogranitic melts.

notes.title: Falling-sphere viscometry at ESRF ID27
notes.body: High-pressure, high-temperature viscosity measurement at the European Synchrotron, tracking a falling marker sphere through a melt under X-ray radiography. The campaign also tested a modified Paris–Edinburgh cell assembly developed for the purpose — a design problem as much as a measurement one, since the cell has to stay transparent to the beam while holding pressure.

notes.title: Falling-sphere viscometry at SOLEIL PSICHE
notes.body: The first of the two falling-sphere campaigns, on the PSICHE beamline at SOLEIL near Paris: a Paris–Edinburgh press in the white beam, a melt at pressure and temperature, and a small sphere whose fall, filmed in X-rays, gives the viscosity directly. Much of the week went into making the new cell assembly behave.

notes.title: Deuterium content and site occupancy in iron sulphide, by in situ neutron diffraction
notes.body: Neutrons see hydrogen where X-rays effectively cannot. Working at J-PARC in Japan, we located deuterium within the iron sulphide structure at high pressure and temperature, and quantified how much it holds. Iron sulphide is a plausible host for hydrogen in planetary cores, which makes its capacity part of the budget for where a planet's water ends up. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth.

notes.title: What controls the oxygen content of sulphide melts in the upper mantle
notes.body: Sulphide inclusions trapped in diamonds carry a record of the conditions under which they grew. This experimental study established how temperature, pressure and composition govern the oxygen dissolved in mantle sulphide melt — the basis for using that oxygen content as a geothermometer. Contributions to Mineralogy and Petrology.

notes.title: The single-crystal diamond trap: reading the composition of high-P–T fluids
notes.body: Fluids move chemistry through the Earth's interior and are almost impossible to sample without changing them on the way out. This method uses a single diamond crystal to trap a fluid at pressure and temperature and recover it intact for analysis, avoiding the contamination and quench problems of the layered-powder traps in general use. Contributions to Mineralogy and Petrology.

notes.title: A modified multi-anvil assembly with a lanthanum chromite heater
notes.body: An 18 mm edge-length assembly redesigned at the Bayerisches Geoinstitut with a thicker LaCrO₃ resistive heater, for longer runs at stable high temperature. Most of experimental petrology is this: the measurement you want is only as good as the small ceramic object you build to make it possible.

notes.title: Sulphur content at sulphide saturation of peridotite melt at upper-mantle conditions
notes.body: How much sulphur a mantle melt can hold before a sulphide liquid separates from it, measured in multi-anvil experiments. The number decides whether sulphur — and the metals that follow it — stays behind in the mantle or travels with the melt. American Mineralogist.

notes.title: In situ neutron diffraction at J-PARC PLANET
notes.body: Six days on BL11 PLANET at the Materials and Life Science Experimental Facility of J-PARC, Japan, the only beamline where a six-axis multi-anvil press (ATSUHIME) sits in a pulsed neutron beam from a spallation source. Hydrogen is almost invisible to X-rays but scatters neutrons strongly, so neutron diffraction is the one way to see where it sits in a crystal structure, and the collimation of the PLANET beam keeps the background low enough to work with deuterium's incoherent scattering. A pellet of FeS was packed in an NaCl capsule between pellets of ND3BD3, which released deuterium on heating, inside a graphite furnace and a Cr-doped MgO cubic cell. Time-of-flight powder patterns were collected at about 3, 7 and 11 GPa and 600–1400 K, with empty-cell runs for background subtraction. Rietveld refinement of the patterns gave the site and occupancy of deuterium in the NiAs-type FeS structure and the volume expansion on hydrogenation, and the recovered samples showed how little of it survives the quench. With D. J. Frost, T. Boffa Ballaran and A. Kurnosov (Bayreuth), H. Terasaki, T. Sakamaki, A. Suzuki and E. Ohtani (Tohoku), and A. Sano-Furukawa and J. Abe (J-PARC). Proposal 2019B.

notes.title: Sulphide–silicate partitioning of W, Mo, Ni and Co at 7–11 GPa
notes.body: If an iron sulphide liquid segregated to the core alongside iron metal, what would it have taken with it? Primitive-mantle peridotite and FeS doped with tungsten, molybdenum, nickel and cobalt were equilibrated in a multi-anvil press at 2,000–2,350 °C in single-crystal MgO capsules, for about five minutes, then analysed by electron microprobe and laser-ablation ICP-MS. Nickel and cobalt follow the sulphide strongly; tungsten barely at all; molybdenum more than tungsten — which is one way to explain the Mo/W ratio of the Earth's mantle. Presented as a poster at the Bayerisches Geoinstitut.

notes.title: Imaging single dislocations in minerals with electron channelling contrast
notes.body: Electron channelling contrast imaging had been used almost only on metals. In an ordinary field-emission SEM, by tilting a crystal by fractions of a degree into a two-beam condition found from its electron backscatter pattern, individual dislocations in deformed ferropericlase and stacking faults in a Moncaup augite were imaged without cutting a TEM foil. Whether a defect shows up depends on the structure factor of the band chosen — a 22 % band showed nothing, a 69 % band showed everything. Became Miyajima et al., European Journal of Mineralogy.
